questions.q: What is the core rule that distinguishes code that belongs in src/ from code that belongs in scripts/?
options: src/ holds Python and scripts/ holds shell scripts
Code other files import from lives in src/; code you just run lives in scripts/
src/ is for GPU code, scripts/ is for CPU code
There is no real difference; it is purely a naming convention
questions.explain: The organizing principle is import vs. run: anything another file imports from belongs in src/ as library code, while one-off runnable scripts belong in scripts/ and should import from src/ rather than duplicate logic.

questions.q: Why do well-run research codebases keep notebooks out of the core src/ package?
options: Notebooks cannot contain Python functions
Notebooks are slower to execute than scripts
Notebook execution order and cell state are unreliable, so load-bearing logic in a notebook is hard to reproduce
Jupyter is not compatible with version control at all
questions.explain: Notebooks are prone to hidden execution order and stale cell state, making them unreliable for anything that must be reproducible. Logic used more than once should graduate into src/.

questions.q: Why is experiments/ kept separate from data/ in the recommended layout?
options: They must be separated because Hydra requires it
data/ holds large or fetched datasets and small fixtures, while experiments/ holds generated run outputs like logs and checkpoints — both get gitignored for different reasons
experiments/ is only used in production, not research
data/ is always committed to git, so it cannot share a folder with outputs
questions.explain: data/ is for fixtures (real datasets live on shared storage or are pulled by a versioning tool), while experiments/ holds per-run generated artifacts. Both are typically gitignored, but for different reasons — size vs. being regenerated.

questions.q: What does pip install -e . accomplish in a research repo's src/ layout?
options: It deletes the existing virtual environment
It installs the local package in editable mode so import my_project works everywhere without reinstalling after changes
It encrypts the source code before committing
It automatically runs the test suite
questions.explain: An editable install lets scripts, notebooks, and tests import the package by name from anywhere in the repo, and immediately reflects any local code changes without a reinstall.

questions.q: According to the 'reproducibility by README' standard, what must be true for a research repo to be considered reproducible?
options: The README must contain a detailed prose explanation of the methodology
The code must achieve state-of-the-art results
A stranger must be able to regenerate the reported result using only the commands in the README, run against a given commit
The repo must have at least 100 GitHub stars
questions.explain: The practical test is whether the README's copy-pasted commands, run from a fresh clone at a known commit, actually regenerate the reported number — not how clean or well-documented the code looks.
